interpretations.rationale: The accessors are consistent views rather than conflicting ones, and the mismatch that could mislead a client is documented at the accessor itself. LastIndex delegates to getLastIndex, which returns the maximum of the stored log index and the snapshot index under the last-index lock (state.go:159-163); CommitIndex returns the committed index; AppliedIndex returns the applied index whose documentation (api.go:1238-1244) states that it reflects the last index sent to the FSM over the apply channel and that the application's state may therefore lag behind it. That caveat matches the write site: processLogs advances the applied index after the batch has been queued to the FSM thread (raft.go:1352-1358), so a client that polls AppliedIndex to decide whether its own write is applied can be told the index before the FSM has processed it, exactly as documented; a client that waits on its own Apply or Barrier future instead is answered by the FSM thread. Snapshot metadata does not use any of these accessors: the FSM thread reports the index it has accounted for with the snapshot request (fsm.go:216-233), and takeSnapshot checks that value against the committed configuration index before creating a snapshot (snapshot.go:125-211), so the fourth value is the one that bounds what a snapshot may claim. Consequences for reading earlier work in this run: the applied index reported by a node is a dispatch watermark, the FSM thread's index is the one that produces snapshot indices, and configuration visibility depends on the append path rather than on either watermark. No defect is claimed.
counterevidence: The strongest candidate for a defect here - an accessor that claims more than it delivers - is explicitly disclaimed in the accessor's own documentation, so a client cannot be misled by the name alone.

Snapshot metadata being produced by the FSM thread rather than by an accessor removes the possibility of a snapshot claiming state the FSM has not reached, which was checked separately in an earlier question with its guard.
limitations: Source-only synthesis; no concurrent measurement of the four values was requested in this turn.
The distance by which AppliedIndex can lead the FSM under a slow application was not measured.
This consolidates vocabulary; it supersedes nothing and changes no earlier conclusion.

interpretations.rationale: Detection and recovery agree in the captured revision. HasExistingState (api.go:460-494) is documented as reporting logs, knowledge of a current term or any snapshot, and the implementation checks exactly those three things in that order: a stable current term above zero returns true, a 'not found' error is ignored while other term errors are propagated, a log last index above zero returns true, and a non-empty snapshot list returns true. NewRaft's documentation (api.go:496-500) states that old state such as snapshots, logs and peers is restored when the node is constructed, so a caller that respects the helper will not bootstrap over data the constructor would recover. The captured test for this contract (raft_test.go:255-295) records the expected direction on both sides: a freshly created node in a merged cluster reports no existing state before it joins, and the same node reports existing state after joining, which matches the helper's use of the stable term and log index. The one durable component the helper does not consult directly is the persisted vote; in both write paths that persist one, the term is raised durably first - the election path raises the term before persisting the vote (raft.go:1983 and 2021), and the vote-handling path adopts a higher term before persisting the vote (raft.go:1668 and 1726) - so a stored vote cannot exist without a non-zero current term, and the first check covers it. The remaining asymmetry is conservative rather than unsafe: a used-but-cleared log store, or a custom store that reports a non-zero last index for a fresh node, makes the helper report existing state, which errs towards recovering rather than bootstrapping. No defect is claimed.
counterevidence: The candidate gap - a persisted vote that the helper ignores - is closed by the durable ordering of the two write paths, not merely by the absence of a counterexample.
The captured test expectation covers both directions (fresh node false, joined node true), so the helper's contract is not only documented but exercised by the package's own tests.
limitations: Source-only; no execution was requested for this question in this turn.
The conservative direction (existing state reported for a cleared but previously used store) was not exercised against a real store.
The vote-order argument covers the write paths present in this revision; it is not a statement about other revisions.

interpretations.rationale: The duties are documented where they are consumed, and the two surprising ones are freedoms rather than obligations. FirstIndex and LastIndex are specified to return 0 when there are no entries, which is what the snapshot and replication code relies on when it decides whether a prefix is available (for example the last-index helper returning the maximum of log and snapshot index). StoreLogs is explicitly permitted to store a batch that is not contiguous with previous logs, and the library uses that gap to mark the discontinuity created by a snapshot restore; stores that cannot tolerate gaps must opt in through MonotonicLogStore.IsMonotonic, after which Raft removes all previous logs instead of relying on the gap. The captured in-memory store inserts entries by index and does not implement the opt-in, so it takes the gap branch - consistent with the fork in the install path that chooses between removing all old logs and compacting. The barrier type carries its own documented contract: it exists so that callers can be sure preceding operations reached the FSM, and it resolves only when the FSM manager acknowledges it, which is stronger than a committed no-op and matches the ordering observed earlier in the apply path. Finally, AppendedAt is disclaimed as a coordination input: it is operational information, followers may see a future timestamp from clock skew, and the leader is not required to persist before delivering log entries, so nothing may treat it as an ordering or freshness signal - a reading worth recording because age metrics are derived from it. No defect is claimed; the one consumer/producer mismatch that would matter belongs to a store implementation that needs monotonicity without declaring it, which is outside the captured snapshot.
counterevidence: The only mismatch found is on the implementation side (a store needing monotonicity without declaring it), and the captured in-memory store correctly takes the gap branch instead of claiming monotonicity.

The barrier contract explains why a Barrier is a stronger synchronisation point than a no-op, which is consistent with the apply-path ordering established separately in this run rather than contradicting it.
limitations: Source-only; no custom store was written and no gap-dependent resynchronisation was executed for this question.
Third-party stores shipped outside this snapshot were not inspected.
The call-site survey covers the paths read in this run (replication, snapshot restore, install, oldest-log metrics), not every use of the store interfaces.

interpretations.rationale: The lossy encoding is established from source; its reachability is not. appendConfigurationEntry chooses the entry format from the leader's protocol version alone: below 2 it appends a deprecated remove-peer entry whose payload is encodePeers(configuration) (raft.go:1219-1233), and encodePeers iterates the configuration taking only servers with suffrage Voter, with the stated reason that other suffrage types are not supported by the data format (configuration.go:311-327). The receiving side is symmetric: the deprecated entry is decoded with decodePeers, which reconstructs every server as a voter (configuration.go:330-352), and the same encoder fills the peers field returned to protocol-version-below-2 voters (raft.go:1620-1622). nextConfiguration had computed the full configuration and checkConfiguration only requires at least one voter, so a non-voter or staging entry in the computed configuration would not stop the append - it would simply not be representable in the written entry. What that means depends entirely on whether the precondition is reachable, and this turn did not establish it: non-voter and staging entries enter only through the versioned configuration format or through a snapshot from a member that used it, so the candidate paths are a deliberate downgrade of a running member, a mixed-version cluster in which the older node becomes leader, and a snapshot restored from a newer member (the version bounds themselves allow protocol 0 and above, config.go:100-106, with the handler accepting one version back). Until one of those is shown to produce a below-2 leader holding such a configuration, this stays a sourced boundary rather than a defect; the decisive test is to append one membership change on such a leader and compare the decoded entry with the configuration the change requested.
counterevidence: A cluster that has only ever run protocol 1 cannot have non-voter or staging entries in its configuration, because the deprecated format cannot introduce them; the concern is confined to downgrade, mixed-version and snapshot-restore states.

checkConfiguration still guarantees at least one voter, so the lossy path cannot produce a configuration with no voters - the risk would be losing non-voting members in the written entry, not losing the quorum.
limitations: No execution: no entry was appended or decoded, and no downgrade or mixed-version cluster was constructed.
Reachability was not established, so no defect is claimed and the question stays paused with its discriminator.
The wider compatibility matrix (which version combinations the library promises to support during rolling upgrades) was not surveyed.

interpretations.rationale: The mechanism is established and the precondition is reachable under a named deployment, so the answer is conditional rather than unresolved. Mechanism: with a leader whose protocol version is below 2, appendConfigurationEntry writes a deprecated remove-peer entry whose payload is encodePeers(configuration) (raft.go:1219-1233), encodePeers keeps only servers whose suffrage is Voter and states that other suffrage types are not supported by the format (configuration.go:311-327), and the receiving side decodes deprecated entries with decodePeers, which reconstructs every server as a voter (configuration.go:330-352) - so a non-voter or staging entry in the computed configuration is written back without it, and nothing on that path reports the loss because checkConfiguration only requires at least one voter. Precondition: a below-2 leader must hold such a configuration. The constructor makes that reachable after a downgrade-style restart: NewRaft rebuilds the configuration by replaying the log through processConfigurationLogEntry (api.go:593-607), which decodes each entry by its own type rather than by the node's configured protocol version, so a node restarted with protocol version 1 keeps a configuration containing non-voters that was originally written in the versioned format; its configuration store, not its protocol version, decides who counts for quorum. The membership API available at that version is the deprecated one - AddPeer refuses when the protocol version is above 2 (api.go:905-919), while the versioned AddVoter/AddNonvoter require protocol 2 or above - so an operator on a downgraded node has precisely the API whose payload cannot carry non-voters. Interoperability does not block the scenario either: the RPC header check accepts one version back (raft.go:45-70), so a protocol-1 node can exchange RPCs with protocol-2 peers that still understand the deprecated entry. Therefore, in a cluster where a member is restarted at a protocol version below 2 (a rollback after a versioned configuration has been written) and that member leads a membership change, the appended entry drops every non-voting member, and every peer decodes it that way. Scope and severity: this is a configuration-fidelity defect conditional on that deployment, it does not endanger quorum, and it does not occur in a cluster that never used the versioned format. Whether a rollback below the version that wrote a configuration is a supported operation is left to the reader; the captured code does not prevent it and does not warn about it.
counterevidence: A cluster that has only ever run protocol 1 cannot hold non-voter entries, because the deprecated format cannot introduce them, so the defect cannot arise there.
checkConfiguration still guarantees at least one voter, so the worst case is losing non-voting members, not losing the ability to commit.
The one-version-back RPC window means the mixed deployment is not obviously excluded by the protocol checks, which is what makes the precondition reachable rather than hypothetical.
limitations: No execution: the appended entry was not decoded and compared, and no downgraded node was constructed.
Whether the library supports rollback below the version that wrote versioned configuration entries is a policy question outside the captured sources.
The conclusion is scoped to a deliberate restart with a lower protocol version on stores that already contain versioned configuration entries.
interpretations.report_title: 降级到 protocol 1 的 leader 会以旧格式写配置条目，非投票成员被静默丢弃
interpretations.report_answer: 条件性确认的缺陷：当 leader 的 protocolVersion 低于 2 时，appendConfigurationEntry 使用旧格式（encodePeers）写成员变更（raft.go:1219-1233），而该编码只保留 Voter，注释明确说明其他 suffrage 不受支持（configuration.go:311-327）；接收端 decodePeers 也只会还原为 Voter（configuration.go:330-352），因此配置中的非投票成员会被静默丢弃，checkConfiguration 只要求至少一个 Voter，不会报错。触发条件：低于 2 的 leader 持有含非投票成员的配置。该前置状态可达：NewRaft 通过回放日志重建配置（api.go:593-607），解码只依赖条目类型、不看本节点协议版本，所以把成员以 protocol 1 重启后仍会保留版本化格式写入的非投票成员；而 protocol 1 下可用的成员变更 API 恰是旧格式的 AddPeer（API 在 protocolVersion > 2 时拒绝，api.go:905-919），RPC 头检查允许一个版本回退（raft.go:45-70），protocol 1 与 protocol 2 节点可以互通。影响范围：属于部署性条件（写出版本化配置后回退版本再重启），不会破坏 quorum，也只在曾使用版本化格式的集群中出现；库是否“支持”这种回退未在快照中说明。

interpretations.rationale: The contract is coherent and the ordering is explicit. Shutdown takes a lock, and on the first call closes the shutdown channel, marks the node shut down, sets the Shutdown state and returns a future bound to the node; a later call returns a future whose raft pointer is nil precisely so that nothing is closed twice (api.go:1012-1025). Because the node is marked and moved to Shutdown before the future is returned, a caller that ignores the future still observes the state change, while a caller that waits obtains the stronger guarantee: the shutdown future's Error waits on the node's routine group and closes the transport when it implements WithClose (future.go:167-180), so the return value is the only thing that waits for background work rather than just requesting it. In-flight operations are not orphaned by the channel closing: the processLogs batch handoff selects on the shutdown channel and responds ErrRaftShutdown to every future in the batch it could not dispatch (raft.go:1300-1310), and the run loops return out of their select when the channel closes so their own pending futures are answered by the cleanup paths already recorded in this run (leadership-lost for the leader's inflight set). No defect is claimed: the two-phase shape, the idempotence and the explicit shutdown responses are consistent with each other, and the only boundary worth naming is that a caller who never waits on the future gets a request rather than a completed shutdown.
counterevidence: The second-call future carries a nil node deliberately, which is what prevents a double transport close rather than being an oversight.
The ordering (mark and change state under the lock, then return the future) means an ignored future cannot leave the node looking healthy.
limitations: Source-only; no shutdown was raced against in-flight operations in this run.
Only the processLogs handoff was cited as an in-flight response path; other shutdown response sites were not enumerated.
Transports without WithClose are awaited but not closed, which was read but not exercised.

interpretations.rationale: The contrast between the two delivery modes is deliberate and visible in a few lines. observe builds one observation per registered observer, applies that observer's filter, skips observers with no channel, and then either sends unconditionally when the observer asked for blocking behaviour or attempts a non-blocking send and increments a dropped counter when the channel is full (observer.go:120-151). The counters are per observer and updated atomically, so a consumer can detect loss rather than infer it. Ordering of registration is guarded separately: RegisterObserver and DeregisterObserver take the observers write lock (observer.go:104-118) while delivery holds only the read lock, so a blocking observer does not prevent another observer from being visited, but a blocking observer does hold the read lock for the duration of its send and therefore blocks registration or deregistration until it returns. Consequences worth stating for a consumer: with the default non-blocking mode, losing observations under load is expected and the drop counter is the signal; with the opt-in blocking mode, the observer can stall whichever internal goroutine emitted the observation - main loop, replication or the FSM thread, depending on the event - and the observation stream must not be treated as a durable log. No defect is claimed: the interface documents that observations are sent when an event occurs and the implementation's drop counting makes the best-effort semantics observable.
counterevidence: A blocking observer cannot cause an internal deadlock by itself: delivery holds only a read lock, so it cannot block another observer's delivery, and the counters let a consumer distinguish loss from silence.
Nothing in the interface promises lossless delivery, so the drop path is a documented-by-design consequence of the non-blocking default rather than an unstated violation.
limitations: Source-only; no observer was registered or saturated in this run.
The blast radius of a blocking observer was reasoned per emitting goroutine but not measured.
The full list of event producers was not enumerated; the observation payload types in the interface are the extent of what was read.

interpretations.rationale: The two layers agree. The API documentation states that Barrier issues a command which blocks until all preceding operations have been applied to the FSM and that it must run on the leader or fail, and it describes the optional timeout as limiting how long we wait for the command to be started (api.go:854-858); the implementation creates a barrier log future with no index or term yet and then selects on the caller's timer while offering the future to the apply channel (api.go:859-880), which is exactly an enqueue bound. The log-level contract recorded earlier says the barrier type exists to ensure preceding operations reached the FSM and resolves only on the FSM manager's acknowledgement (log.go:33-38), which is what makes the successful completion meaningful. Consequences for a caller: a success means the FSM reflects all preceding writes; a timeout means the command was not started in time, so the caller must not read it as 'not yet applied' versus 'applied' - it simply does not know; and a non-leader returns the not-leader error rather than queueing the barrier. No defect is claimed; the only boundary worth naming is that the timeout is an enqueue deadline, which the documentation states explicitly.
counterevidence: The candidate confusion - treating the timeout as an application deadline - is explicitly excluded by the documentation's wording and by the implementation's enqueue-time select.
The completion semantics are anchored twice: at the API and at the log type, so a caller following either is not misled.
limitations: Source-only; no barrier timeout was raced against a slow FSM in this run.
Apply latency after a successful enqueue was not measured.
The follower rejection path was not re-read here; it follows the same not-leader rule recorded elsewhere in this run.
